name: Gamma Correction Trace
description: Detects gamma correction traces by estimating applied gamma curves — multiple gamma corrections indicate manipulation.
mechanism:
This method detects traces of gamma correction in images, which reveals processing history and can indicate image manipulation or AI generation:

1. **Intensity Histogram Analysis**: Gamma correction I_out = I_in^γ creates characteristic patterns in the intensity histogram. The method analyzes the histogram for periodic peaks and valleys (combing artifacts) that appear when discrete pixel values are remapped through a power-law curve. For γ < 1 (brightening), gaps appear in the dark tones; for γ > 1 (darkening), gaps appear in the highlights.

2. **Gamma Parameter Estimation**: Using the method of Farid (2001), the gamma value is estimated by computing the bispectral correlation of the intensity distribution. The bispectrum of a gamma-corrected signal exhibits a phase shift proportional to (γ − 1). The estimated γ value reveals: single camera processing (γ ≈ 1/2.2 = 0.45 for sRGB), re-encoded images (γ ≈ 0.45² = 0.2, double gamma), or AI-generated content (no consistent gamma signature).

3. **Regional Gamma Consistency**: The image is divided into 128×128 blocks and the local gamma is estimated for each block. Authentic single-capture images show consistent gamma across all regions (coefficient of variation CV < 0.1). Composited or manipulated images show gamma inconsistencies between spliced regions. AI-generated images typically show either no gamma signature or irregular local gamma patterns.

4. **Double Gamma Detection**: When an image undergoes gamma correction twice (e.g., camera gamma + editing software), the intensity histogram shows a distinct double-combing pattern with aliased peaks at predictable positions. The method detects this by computing the autocorrelation of the histogram and looking for secondary peaks at intervals corresponding to the gamma-transformed spacing.
parameters:
Block size: 128×128 pixels for local gamma estimation
Bispectral analysis: 256-bin histogram
Gamma range: 0.1–5.0
Consistency threshold: CV < 0.15 for authentic images
Double-gamma detection: autocorrelation peak threshold > 0.3
Minimum image size: 256×256 pixels
accuracy: 78–86% accuracy in detecting gamma manipulation traces. Double-gamma detection achieves 90% on re-encoded images. Regional gamma consistency analysis reaches 83% for splice detection. AI-generated image detection based on gamma absence achieves 75%. JPEG compression reduces accuracy by 5–8% at quality < 85.
source: Farid, H. (2001). Blind Inverse Gamma Correction. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 10(10), 1428–1433.
useCase: Detecting image manipulation by identifying inconsistent gamma correction across regions. Verifying processing history through gamma trace analysis. Detecting AI-generated images that lack authentic camera gamma signatures. Identifying re-encoded or multiply-processed images through double-gamma detection.
strengths:
• Based on well-understood signal processing principles (power-law transforms)
• Histogram combing artifacts are robust forensic indicators
• Regional gamma analysis provides spatial localization of manipulated regions
• Can reconstruct the processing history (number of gamma corrections applied)
• Complementary to other processing trace methods (JPEG artifact analysis, noise analysis)
limitations:
• High-bit-depth processing (16-bit) reduces histogram combing artifacts
• Dithering applied during gamma correction can mask combing patterns
• Very dark or very bright images have insufficient dynamic range for reliable estimation
• Some AI generators apply sRGB gamma during output, mimicking authentic camera gamma
• Adaptive tone mapping (HDR processing) creates complex non-power-law curves
